source.title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
source.authors: Tavish Mankash; Vardhaman Kalloli; Keshava Prasad; Deepan Muthirayan

record.tranche_reason: The study uses different interpretability measures and causal interventions to assess whether a model’s native coordinates are readable and usable directly. It does not reproduce the original Qwen3 neuron-pole audit.
record.gate_note: The paper reports native-coordinate specificity, causal ablations, coordinate transfer, and a fixed-coordinate steering policy. These results bear on architecture-related coordinate readability (V4) and direct use of native coordinates as analysis or intervention units (V5). Detector-only classification scores are not included as rows because they measure request detection rather than whether coordinates explain model behavior. No results establish the fraction of neurons with one or two jobs, or test explanations by simulating their predicted activations on new text.
record.test_reason: The study compares, at matched compute, how readable FFN-update output coordinates are in Dense, Standard MoE and MoWE models, and traces one prediction through MoWE's own coordinates without a replacement model. This bears loosely on V4 (architecture shapes readability) and V5 (native units as circuit units). The unit differs from V4's neurons. In Dense and Standard MoE, FFN-update coordinates are residual-basis directions with no privileged basis, not hidden neurons. In MoWE, each coordinate is one expert's output by construction. The readability measure is a mean specificity score, not a share of interpretable neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add: standard MoE reaches the lowest loss, but its native coordinates are no more readable than a random rotation. The authors attribute the readability gain to disjoint output writing, not sparse routing. MoWE also beats Dense on evaluation cross-entropy (2.417 vs 2.452).
record.recipe_differences: The paper introduces and evaluates a new routed architecture, MoWE, and uses judge-scored coordinate descriptions, randomized basis controls, and selected causal interventions. It does not reproduce the Qwen3-32B pole audit or its job-count categories.
record.method_sensitivity: The main coordinate-specificity results vary by architecture and representation (native, rotated, or SAE). In the rectangle-prompt intervention, strength 1.5 is the first tested value at which degrees becomes the top prediction. The request steering packet and detector cutoffs are selected separately for each model.

fits_no_version.finding: Site-matched TopK SAEs raise specificity more for Dense (0.375→0.489) than for MoWE (0.523→0.556). Native MoWE is comparable to the Dense SAE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An architecture with a privileged, write-disjoint output basis yields native coordinates about as readable as post-hoc SAE features on a dense model.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixed native-coordinate packets steer next tokens in MoWE (angle→degrees; 99/100 hazardous refusals, 9/100 benign). The Dense packet converts 0/86 detected hazards.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Native coordinates of a write-disjoint architecture serve as reusable steering handles where dense output coordinates do not.

fits_no_version.finding: At 512 scale, layer-6 coordinates scoring >0.7 purity are 4% (MoE) and 22% (Dense). Scores come from a judge on high-activation contexts, not simulation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Only a minority of native output coordinates get high judge-scored purity on held-out top-activating contexts.

record.problems: The all-layer interpretability audit uses one checkpoint per architecture; the loss comparison has two runs per architecture. The judge-based specificity measure is not a reported share of coordinates passing a job-count threshold. The case studies use selected examples, and request steering measures only the next token in one narrow request family. The largest evaluated model has 363.7M parameters.
record.rows_left_out: Detector-only request-classification results in Table 5 were omitted because they measure hazard detection rather than coordinate-based explanation or causal reconstruction. Sign-reversal and matched-random packet results in Table 6 were not separately recorded; the combined policy outcomes and coordinate-transfer control are included.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and no one-job/two-job/unexplained shares.
No job-count shares in other models. Largest model is 363.7M parameters.
No vision models, no cat-and-car neuron, no test of recursive generalization.
No share of interpretable hidden neurons. No InceptionV1-sized estimates. Regularization and capacity not isolated. 'Better tools' for neurons not tested; SAEs are replacement bases.
No attribution graphs, no large model, no comparison with a replacement model's reconstruction error, and only a single selected prompt.
Descriptions are scored only on other high-activation contexts; no test of predicting where coordinates fire versus do not fire.
No simulation-based scoring of activations on new text.

missing.what: 512-scale standard MoE vs Dense layer-6 purity and specificity (0.193 vs 0.388; fraction >0.7: 0.04 vs 0.22)
Controlled known-cause task: MoWE has higher coordinate and slice purity than MoE and Dense at equal accuracy
10-layer pilot native-minus-rotation purity: MoWE 0.257 vs Dense 0.033

record.verdict_notes: Main caveat: the measured unit is the FFN output coordinate. In Dense and Standard MoE this is a residual-basis direction with no privileged basis, so parity with random rotation is expected. The comparison is largely privileged-by-construction vs non-privileged bases, not neurons across architectures. One checkpoint per architecture was audited, the judge is a single LLM, and the case studies are selected examples.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or one-job/two-job/ununderstood proportions.
The study compares small Dense, Standard MoE, and MoWE models, but does not measure the claimed job-count shares across models or scale to trillions of parameters.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.

Tests differences in coordinate-specificity scores across architectures, not the claimed percentage of interpretable neurons, the InceptionV1-sized model estimates, or the separate effects of tools and regularization.
Tests narrow native-coordinate tracing and interventions, not attribution graphs for a large model, full behavioral reconstruction, or reconstruction error.
Descriptions are tested on separate high-activation contexts; the study does not test whether they predict where coordinates fire across positive and negative examples.
The judge scores descriptions against held-out activating passages; it does not simulate predicted activations on new text or report the fraction of neurons above a good-score threshold.

tranche.reason: A new architecture is evaluated on the readability question with a different method: LM-judge coordinate specificity with shuffled-description and rotation controls.

source_check.notes: Readability is LM-judge specificity of FFN-update output coordinates, audited on one checkpoint per architecture (two training runs each). Rankings depend on the shuffled-floor correction: by raw purity, Standard MoE ranks highest (0.630 vs MoWE 0.601, Dense 0.573). Standard MoE uses k=38 of 768 experts, with 3.3% more MACs and 32.6% more parameters than MoWE.

statements.correction: MoWE 0.523 vs Dense 0.375, difference 0.148, CI [0.095, 0.204]. MoWE is higher than Dense and Standard MoE in 18 of 19 layers. MoWE rotation 0.384.
statements.problem: MoWE numbers are right. MoWE has 2.65 times Dense's parameters at matched active compute. Only one checkpoint per architecture was audited, although two runs of each were trained.

statements.correction: Standard MoE 0.268 vs Dense 0.375 (difference 0.107, CI [0.031, 0.184]). Rotation 0.289. Native minus rotation -0.021, CI [-0.065, 0.023].

This study's Standard MoE has G=768 experts with k=38 active (about 5%), H=8, and full-width expert outputs. Specificity 0.268 vs Dense 0.375 (Dense minus MoE 0.107, CI [0.031, 0.184]). Rotation 0.289 (native minus rotation -0.021, CI [-0.065, 0.023]). It uses 3.3% more active MACs and 32.6% more parameters than MoWE. One checkpoint per architecture was audited.
statements.problem: The numbers are right. But the suggestion that routing sparsity may separate the cases does not fit this study: its Standard MoE is very sparse and still scores below Dense.

statements.correction: Not isolated for LM readability: regularization, capacity.
statements.problem: The paper does not isolate regularization or capacity as causes of readability. Router regularization is varied only in a toy appendix (A.2), measured by routing MI, and in the LM router screen, measured by loss.

Degrees probability falls from 0.715 to 0.670 after joint ablation.

On one prompt, MoWE zeroes each of 722 active coordinates and records a 722 x 722 influence matrix over later coordinates. It reports one selected four-coordinate path: coordinate-to-coordinate drops 0.90, 0.84, 1.42 and a coordinate-to-logit drop 0.74. No full graph is reported or scored for faithfulness.
statements.problem: The statement implies MoWE has no unit-to-unit edges. It does measure coordinate-to-coordinate ablation edges, though it builds no attribution graph.
